Q: How do threat modeling and trust boundaries guide security controls for an AI app?
A:
Threat modeling systematically identifies protected assets (vector embeddings, proprietary documents, API keys, customer conversations), untrusted actors (external callers, prompt-injecting web pages, compromised third-party plugins), entry points (REST/SSE endpoints, MCP transports, file upload parsers), and critical trust boundaries across the AI pipeline. Rather than relying on vague, unquantifiable instructions like 'make the system secure', threat modeling translates security goals into deterministic, verifiable architectural controls.

The most critical boundary in AI systems separates untrusted natural language data (user queries, scraped HTML, and retrieved database chunks) from authoritative system instructions and backend tool execution engines. Because modern LLMs process system instructions and retrieved context within the same shared token stream, readable text must never inherit execution authority. Threat modeling enforces defense-in-depth: (1) authenticating identity at ingress via signed tokens or mTLS; (2) authorizing tool actions at the server dispatch boundary using least-privilege capability tokens and strict parameter validation; (3) enforcing tenant isolation at the database layer through mandatory server-injected WHERE clauses; and (4) restricting outbound network egress to prevent data exfiltration via SSRF. Teams must continuously test bypass scenarios—such as indirect injection payloads and cross-tenant citation requests—in automated CI pipelines rather than relying solely on probabilistic safety guardrails or system prompt wording.
Why: A retrieved document tells an agent to upload customer records to a URL. The document may be readable evidence, but it has no authority to grant network destinations or permission to export private records.
Risk: Conflating readable content with executable authority creates an injection path.
Trade: Limit powerful operations and preserve useful read behavior behind explicit policy.
Try: Draw the boundary between retrieved text, proposed tool arguments and an authorized effect.
